subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: But a man may have a permit to build a cabin or a small house, and he has no lease or anything else. In other words he is in the position where a licence may be repealed at any moment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: No, he can have a licence up to 21 years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: In other words, a licence is the same thing as a lease?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: The difference between a licence and a lease is that a lease grants exclusive possession while a licence does not. Somebody can pass over a property which is not in anyone's exclusive possession.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: I would urge the minister to look into that matter, because people who may be in that situation, or may subsequently get into that situation, are in little better position than they would be in the case of a licence. At the present time there are a certain number of these cases. In future there may be a much larger number of cases, particularly if these parks develop, as I trust and hope they will, into very large skiing resorts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
I want to ask the minister a question relating to lake Louise hotel. I am not referring to the fence we have heard criticized so much, although I think this is regrettable because the hotel had been up for many years without any fence being around the property, and then all of a sudden they decide to build a fence and it has caused a great deal of criticism. No doubt the reason given was that tourists were leaving a lot of wastepaper, etc., around the grounds, but I asked the superintendent of the park at Banff whether park officials had had any difficulty in that regard where there are public grounds and where tourists wander in crowds, and he said they had had no difficulty. There may be some reason in the case of the hotel but is it necessary to build a fence around the property?
I am wondering how far the lease goes. Does it go right down to the edge of the lake, because not only have they put a fence right around the property but they have also fenced the pathway down around the lake, and have put up a gate and a sign stating "Private Property-No Admittance". I was there in the fall and a lot of people were reluctant to use the walk around the lake because they were afraid they might be trespassing on private property. Surely it is not the intention of the government to fence people off from the lake entirely!

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
I already said, I believe, that according to my information that fence does not exclude the public from the lake shore.

There is a public walk along the entire lake frontage which is accessible by public roadway.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
That is why the lease should be examined. I was up there in September and there was a gate from the fence down to the water's edge. That gate was open, it is true, but there was a large sign reading, "Private Property-No	Admittance". If
people took no notice of that sign they would be able to go along the lake shore but that sign should be removed and the gate and fence around the lake down to the water's edge should be removed and that pathway left open.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for the information he has given me, and I will certainly look into it immediately.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with these leases in town sites such as Banff, Jasper and so on. How long is it since the regulations governing the type of buildings which may be constructed and the other regulations have been revised? I ask this question particularly in view of the fact that I have had a considerable number of complaints from people who had secured lots or intended to secure lots and then found that the building regulations were such that they were not able to put up what you might call a reasonably priced cabin or summer residence.
There has been, I think, on the part of quite a number of people who are in the moderate income class a considerable demand for certain lands around Banff particularly and, I think to some extent, around Jasper, to be set aside where the building regulations would be less extreme than they are at the present time.
83276-53J
National Parks Act
There is no idea on the part of any of these people or on the part of anyone, I think, that there should be erected in the parks anything in the nature of shacks which would detract from the natural beauty of the parks. However, it is quite possible to construct, for considerably less than the amount the regulations have provided for, a cabin of a rustic nature which does not detract from the general appearance of things in the park. Such a cabin can be constructed for considerably less than the amount specified at the present time. I would suggest that the minister look into that matter and, if possible, make changes in the regulations which would accommodate the very people who should find it possible to construct summer homes in our national parks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
I wish to make a remark or two with regard to this section, subsection (j). I understand that the minister will be visiting the national parks during the-course of the next year. When he pays a visit to Riding Mountain national park T suggest that he look at the problem of accommodation for people who enter that park by bus. I will not say anything at length; with regard to this park, because the hon.. member for Brandon-Souris made some comment on it the other day. However, I should like to direct the minister's attention to a section of our populace which perhaps tends to be forgotten or neglected in connection with that particular national park. I refer to those who enter the park by bus.
A large number of people do enter that park by bus. Over the years no very suitable-accommodation has been provided for them. Their numbers run into hundreds. There is; a good bus service into Riding Mountain park from Dauphin, from Minnedosa, from Brandon and from the city of Winnipeg. Particularly on week ends and on holidays during the summer season hundreds of people come there by bus and of course have to leave in the same way. Those who travel to the park by motor car naturally are not faced with this problem.
On many occasions I have made the trip by bus. I am surprised that up to this point no arrangements of a satisfactory nature have been made for people who travel by that means of transportation. What has been done, certainly since the war, in the period that I am thinking of now, is this. The people who have to purchase their tickets for bus travel or to wait for a bus have to do so just at a garage. Those who operate that garage have given efficient service all these years, but they have not the necessary accommodation for those who are waiting. In bad weather people who are waiting for the

National Parks Act
bus to arrive have no place in which to take shelter. There is plenty of space in the park for a bus depot to be constructed.
This is a matter which should have received attention years ago. I hope the minister will take note of it and look into it when he is there. The people who enter our national parks by bus are deserving of the same treatment as those who have other means of transportation. We often think in terms of visitors from the United States and others who are coming in by motor car, but our own people who live sufficiently close to national parks to get there by bus should receive as good treatment as anyone else. In Riding Mountain national park I think that type of person has been forgotten.
It is not out of the way to suggest that the department consider arranging for a proper bus depot where people would have rest rooms; a place in which to take shelter when they are waiting for the bus to come in; a place in which to put their luggage, which they now have to place out in a lane; a place with suitable arrangements for those who are waiting for guests to arrive or who are speeding the parting guest after a holiday. I urge the minister to put that matter down in his notebook as one to observe when he reaches Riding Mountain national park.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext: I am quite ready to put it down in my notebook; but on the other hand I thought it was the practice for transportation companies to build their own depots. I have always thought that was the practice. In my province, anyway, the bus companies build their own depots. I have been through Jasper park and Banff park. In the first, the Canadian National Railways builds its own station. In Banff it is the Canadian Pacific Railway. I would find it quite odd if the C.P.R. were to ask us to build their depot, if you want to call it a depot, or their station in Banff. We would say, "That is your business; you had better build it yourself." I believe the bus companies should do the same in Riding Mountain national park. However, I will of course look into the matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PARKS
speechtext:
It matters not to me who provides this type of accommodation. Perhaps the minister is quite correct in saying the bus people should do that. My point is that someone should look into the matter and see that it is done. After all, the buses are deriving a good revenue from taking people into this park. If they are not providing suitable accommodation, that matter should be drawn to their attention. How is it best to be done? I think certainly by the department which has authority over those national parks. At the present time it is a matter which is being neglected.

I did what I was able to do a few years ago in urging people to provide a direct bus line from the city of Winnipeg to Riding Mountain national park instead of a system under which it was necessary to make changes en route; and that effort turned out very successfully. I am now pressing this second point with regard to a suitable bus depot. After all, the department permits the buses to come in there and it permits the buses to stand on vacant ground, on the roadway or in the lane. Why not insist that they provide proper parking accommodation for their buses and, at the same time, a bus depot?

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was speaking on Bill No. 29. This measure is probably more important than appears on the surface because I would think that most likely it has been drafted very hastily, and I am not sure that it even conveys what the minister wished it to convey when he introduced it, or whether it will accomplish what he anticipates it is going to accomplish. In fact I think he said the other day that he did not know what it was going to accomplish, and I am not surprised because when you read it you realize how hastily it was drawn, and the rest of us have as much doubt as the minister. It looks like a gunshot prescription, knowing the patient is in trouble but not being quite sure what the reaction is going to be. I sometimes wonder why the minister needs to say so much and probably undo what he is trying to do.
I think the bill is intended to help manufacturers in his own particular district because, while many manufacturers in other parts of the country are affected, especially in the textile industry, I think they are more vociferous in the district the minister represents; and after all, charity begins at home. But I think a little more time might well have been spent in studying what repercussions and what benefits may be expected from such an amendment. I do not believe it should be confined entirely to manufactured goods. I think semi-finished goods

and raw products may need attention before very long; and while this is not a matter of high tariffs, protective policy, or even free trade-which has been forgotten by almost everyone-while it does not involve these major fiscal principles it is a matter of whether we are going to continue to be a dumping ground for United States products.
I am not surprised that the minister at last is alarmed. People in this country have been fearful for some time that this development and trend would become more conspicuous when defence requirements fell off. The government have been very fortunate. They have been able to flounder along so far as trade is concerned for the last number of years without any fiscal policy. I do not think the minister can tell us what the fiscal policy of his party is. It is just as uncertain as the effects of this amendment. But like Micawber the government is always waiting for something to turn up, and it has been turning up in the form of large demands for our raw products.
We have been a great accommodation to the United States of America. At times they think we are not producing uranium as fast as we should. At other times they propose to put embargoes on our lead and zinc, and at other times they propose to subsidize their wheat in competition with our wheat throughout the world. But we are very good neighbours, we love them, and we are a very handy and friendly people so far as they are concerned, especially in matters of trade. But when we consider normal trade we find that our great customers-

Yes, it is a half. I notice that in the last six months Canada has bought from the United States $587 million more than we sold them. We had an adverse balance of trade with the world in the first eight months of 1953 of $206 million, and in the same eight months of 1952 we had a favourable trade balance with the world generally of $252 million. Therefore while imports are only part of it, they have been more than half so far as we are concerned. We are buying much more per capita from the United States than the United States is buying from us, even though we have fewer than 15 million people.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is a point I am entitled to make. This amendment is, I think, defined purposely to assist our textile manfacturers in marketing their products in Canada in competition with cheaper goods imported from the United States of America. I realize that it deals only with that one country, and I realize as well that our whole trade problem is seriously affected by the dumping of goods, whether they are offseason or otherwise. I do not know why the bill is confined merely to off-season goods. Section 1 reads in part as follows:
. . . where the market price of any manufactured goods in the country of export has, as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period, declined to levels that do not reflect in the opinion of the minister their normal price . . .
I do not know why it should be confined merely to the advance of the season or the marketing period. I hope amendments might be considered which are not confined to manufactured goods. I realize there are many other lines of goods in this country that are seriously affected.
We have regard for the Geneva arrangement. I believe the minister made the statement that the tariffs and trade agreements might be left as they are for at least another year until the larger countries knew where they were going, not only with regard to matters of trade policy but also matters of finance and payments. Evidently the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did not

Customs Act
know at that time where they were going, because previous to that those countries had pretty well fixed their fiscal policies. Since that time we have experienced all sorts of effects on our products, such as our dairy products, and now there is the rumoured effect of United States action on our coarse grains.
I submit that this amendment might be altered to make it better than it is. Even then I doubt if it would do as effective a job as the minister hopes it might. I do think we have great possibilities in Canada. However, when we have less than 15 million people, and when about a quarter of our so-called trade is dependent on exports, our home markets are very important. When there is any action that relates to our tariff policies in general, I think then the least we can do is appreciate that the dumping of goods which will create unemployment for our Canadian workmen is of vital concern to all in this house. Our standard of living in Canada is dependent so much more on trade than that of the great republic to the south of us, which only exports about 6 per cent of its national production.
I realize there are other products than those that are manufactured. I suppose that so long as the word "manufactured" is in this proposed amendment, Mr. Speaker, you would probably question the relevancy of my remarks if I were to mention those other products. I shall, therefore, endeavour not to embarrass either of us in that regard. Today we see plants closing down, being dismantled, and labouring men thrown out of work in Ontario. In several centres textile plants are closed down entirely. I understand that in one city in Quebec there are between 1,200 and 1,500 men unemployed at the present time. I believe the minister would tell us if he cared to, but he says he does not want me to speak for him, that in his own riding some 300 workers have recently been let out.
Perhaps that fact had something to do with the hurried drafting of this bill. I would not say it was recklessly drafted, but it might have been worded better even if it had been recklessly drafted. In my opinion there are many loopholes, and as it is worded the bill will not serve the purpose intended.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I intend to support it for what it is worth. I am sorry that it is worded as it is. I should like to see the minister give some consideration to altering it now that he has had time to consider the matter. I am not going to detain the house any longer, except to suggest that in this country we need a careful review of our trade policies. I feel that our

country is facing a very critical period, yet we are more or less nonchalantly saying to larger countries like the United Kingdom and the United States that we are not making any changes; we are going to live according to our understanding at the Geneva conference for another year or more. I believe the trend in our trade is now so serious that our people are becoming alarmed. I think the people who are most alarmed are the great body of consumers who, after all, are the producers and workers in this country.
I hope this amendment may do something toward restoring employment, which is so seriously menaced by the lack of sound application of 'our dumping laws. I think it is due to the lack of a sound trade policy that we have so many men unemployed today, and have an unfavourable trade balance such as we have not experienced in any other eight-month period in Canada's history. It is startling, when we are talking about our great prosperity, to find that in this textile industry we have signs of increasing unemployment and mounting adverse balances of trade. Mr. Speaker, Canada needs a trade policy.

In his
remarks last night the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) placed his finger on the underlying problem that is facing this house whenever it comes to examining legislation of this sort, and that is the dual role played by the vast majority of Canadian citizens, not of course excluding members of parliament. He mentioned that the same people are, at the same time, producers and consumers. It is a difficult problem for this parliament to hold the balance between the interests of individuals in their capacity as producers and in their capacity as consumers. It may be, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat has told us, that in one specific industry in this country there are many factories which are closing down or working on part-time operations because of the dumping of similar commodities from other parts of the world.
We have to take into consideration that this legislation will be appealed to not merely by the textile industry which, despite its black record as the leader of this group pointed out last night, may be in this serious condition. We can be quite sure that in the not too distant future there will be many applications from other sections of our economy for the protection of this legislation. If we can judge from the speeches made by the members of the official opposition, those applications will receive vigorous support in this house.

I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is a simple way by which the government may ensure that it is holding a proper balance between the conflicting interests of the Canadian people as consumers and as producers, and that is to see that the interests of Canadian citizens as consumers are not sacrificed to the interests of certain Canadian citizens as producers. That is, whenever an application for protection under this legislation is received by the government from any industry, that industry should be required to open its books to inspection by the government in order that its real financial and economic position may be determined. Moreover, the results of that investigation should be tabled in this house for the examination of hon. members.
That is a reasonable request, because all the arguments that are usually advanced against the production of the books of account of industries, which usually boil down to the fact that it is not fair that the competitors of that industry should be given confidential information about the cost of operation, would fall to the ground in the case of any applications received by virtue of this legislation, since we can be sure that in any case where an application is made it will be made by the entire industry. It will not be one corporation, because they will all be affected by the existing conditions. It is only fair that the Canadian people should be informed of the precise financial position of any section of our economy that asks for protection under this legislation.
We have to remember, sir, that in effect what we are doing, when we grant this protection, is taking money from the pockets of the Canadian consumers by denying them cheap products from outside Canada. Before we do that we must be sure that the moneys we take from their pockets in this way go into the pockets of the general consumers of Canada and not into the pockets of a selected few. Therefore while, like the leader of this group, I am certainly prepared to support any legislation which will prevent the unfair dumping of goods on our markets and cause unemployment of Canadian workers, I would be dubious about supporting such legislation if I thought that at any time in the future it might be used to bolster the financial position and the profit position of certain industries in Canada, to the detriment of the consumers of this country.

speechtext:
I do not
intend to delay the house very long, but there are certain remarks that I feel I should make in regard to this bill. It can be said that it proposes to give some additional protection to the industries of this country. That is on the basis, of course, of protecting them against dumping, which has been recognized as a proper thing to do even by people who believe in a great deal of freedom of trade.
But one of the things I should like to draw to the attention of the minister is the question as to what extent the present protection that is enjoyed by our industries is actually being used solely to protect and build up Canadian industries and give employment to Canadian employees, and to what extent it is being used to exploit the consumers and build up profits in the hands of certain manufacturing industries. This is a matter that must receive very careful consideration at the present time in connection with any bill to increase protection, particularly in some of these industries that are involved in this particular legislation.
Any of us who visit the United States know the difference in the price of electrical goods, cars, trucks and cement. Then there was the recent case of the rubber companies. One can only judge by what has happened in the administration of the Combines Investigation

Customs Act
Act. Under this act twelve rubber companies were found guilty of the infringement of certain provisions, and the judge involved said they had been guilty of cold-blooded, calculated violation of the law. The solicitor acting for the government estimated that they had taken from the consumers illegally over $1 million a year for 15 years.
It is not clear that that statement is actually substantiated by the facts; it may have been exaggerated. Nevertheless these people were found guilty of a combination under which prices were held up improperly. It is also clear that it would have been very hard for them to do that if it were not for the protective tariff. That was taken into consideration when the tariff was passed in the first place, and section 16 provided that if prices were being held up unduly the tariff would either be reduced or cancelled, or a special excise tax put on so they could not take advantage of the tariff to exploit the consumers improperly.
If this action on the part of the rubber companies has been going on for 15 years it indicates that there must be some lack of liaison in this matter between some of the branches of government. It does not help the consumers very much for these people to be brought before the courts and fined. If one group of companies have been doing it, perhaps others have been doing it. It seems to me that one of the objects should be to prevent this thing happening, instead of attempting to punish them after it has happened.
I do suggest that there should be some very close contact between the combines investigation branch and the administration of customs duties to make sure that this sort of thing is not going on. It is one of the things that I suggest should be given very careful study.
In this particular instance power is being given to the minister to decide what is the average price of goods which are imported: . . . weighted as to quantity, at which the like or similar goods were sold for consumption in the country of export during a reasonable period, not exceeding six months, immediately preceding the date of shipment of the goods to Canada.
One of the things I wonder about is how the minister is going to set these prices. Suppose somebody goes and buys some goods in the United States; dress goods, we will say. The suggestion is that there should be an arbitrary fixing of values for the minister. Then he is under obligation to calculate what the average price was in the United States during a period of time of up to six months. 
He cannot take the average price day by day; he must figure out what was likely sold on each of those days at those prices. I think that is a very big job the minister is going to have on his hands if he is going to administer this act. I do not see how he is going to be able to do it.
While we on this side have great confidence in the minister and this government, this legislation could be used to strangle trade, in the hands of a minister who wanted to strangle trade. We are passing this law and putting it on our statute books, and at some time it may be in the hands of a minister who did not belong to a party which believed in promoting trade. It might be in the hands of a minister who believed in strangling trade.
Let me point out how it could be used. If someone went down and bought a quantity of goods at a certain price and then brought them into this country they might be subject to this special duty. Then an investigation would be made and it would take some time to find out what the prices were during the previous six months and how much had likely been sold during that period at those respective prices. At the same time a ruling would be given.
In the meantime this person either would have to keep his goods and refrain from selling them, and the ruling could be held up for a considerable period; or he could go ahead and sell them and take a chance. Then if a ruling was handed down that a substantial duty was payable by way of dumping duty the person might find he had incurred a tremendous loss on this particular transaction. If that sort of thing were going to be held over people buying for importation into Canada they would be afraid to buy goods to which this law might be applied.
In other words a minister who wanted to strangle trade could absolutely strangle it by using this bill in a ruthless way. That is something I think should be brought forward at this time, particularly when we are complaining to the United States that they should stop this uncertainty in regard to goods imported into their country.
We have heard of cases where people have come up here and bought goods such as stoves, have taken them down there and then later on the department has ruled that they belonged in another classification altogether and the person has had such a heavy duty imposed that he had a tremendous loss. The result is that the word goes around that it is unsafe to buy anything in Canada because you do not know what duty you are subsequently going to have to pay.

We have said that is not consistent with the agreement we have had with the United States and that they should, if they really intend to show they mean business in promoting trade, cease this business of having trade subject to uncertainties and rulings which can be made by the minister, which means you cannot ascertain ahead of time just what you are going to have to pay in duty.
We have been making representations like that to the United States government, that our exports into that country should not be subject to these rulings which in effect are strangling our exports to the United States. I presume we are pressing very strongly that they should cease to put discriminatory tariffs against our dairy goods. There is a suggestion now that they will put on tariffs against our oats and I believe against our rye.
People are talking about the necessity of protecting the industries of eastern and central Canada. We are interested in them, too. But as I pointed out to hon. members if we get a trade war started, if we start putting on tariffs, then without question other countries will feel justified in putting on tariffs against our exports. The whole thing will pile up worse than it ever did before. Surely if we ever had an example of the inability of Canada to promote employment in Canada by the use of tariffs we experienced it in the unfortunate days of the early thirties.
If we interfere with exports of our primary products from this country, then no matter how much you put on in the way of tariffs to protect the industries of this country, the people are not going to have the purchasing power they should have. That is one of the things that should never be lost sight of. It is one of those things that may look like an innocent step, but it can be used as an excuse by people promoting similar ideas in the United States to stick by the interferences they have already introduced in regard to imports into the United States, and to introduce more.
They are smarter at that sort of thing, at interfering with imports and protecting their own industries, than we can ever expect to be. If we start engaging in competition like that and justifying them in maintaining their present interferences and extending them we will be embarking upon a course of which we do not know the ultimate end.
The position in which I feel myself to be in regard to this situation is that in the first place I certainly want to take into consideration the situation that is alleged to exist due to this so-called dumping in regard to some 83276-54
Customs Act
of the industries in the central part of Canada. When we are in difficulties we expect to get consideration from other parts of Canada. If we are going to be fair we have to look at the request of the central part of Canada. So when it is said that this is a case of really stopping dumping one is inclined to feel that he should fall in line with it as such.
There is one difficulty, one implication in this thing and one possibility if it gets into the hands of a minister who wants to strangle trade. We are passing this law, and it will be the law of our country for years to come. It gives an excuse to other countries to do the same sort of thing. If it is in the hands of an administration that is inclined to strangle trade, they could use similar regulations to interfere with trade apart from the ordinary ad valorem tariff.
When we consider that there is a problem like this, should we not stop and wonder if we are not starting the same course that we started in the early thirties when as a result of the United States, Canada and other countries raising their tariffs, we prevented manufacturing being carried on in other countries of Europe, we created unemployment there, they refused to take our products and the time came when we could not sell our wheat and great home markets were lost to the central part of Canada.
One reason I have felt that the Liberal party has had such support from the people of Canada is that it has shown itself to be the party that believes in expanding trade. The people as a whole believe that the expansion of trade is the basis of preserving liberties in the world at large, that anything which tends to curtail trade is a retrograde step. This policy was laid down in the speech from the throne in the following succinct sentence:
My ministers are convinced that nations can best achieve economic strength and security through more liberal trade and overseas investment policies and they are continuing their efforts to bring about the progressive reduction of trade restrictions.
I believe that is a true statement of fundamental economic wisdom. That is the reason, I think, the Liberal party has been kept in power steadily ever since 1935. The people of Canada came to the conclusion that restriction of trade was a mistake, that while you can justify it in certain individual cases the ultimate result is bad for the economy as a whole because other people do the same sort of thing.
Most people felt that, as we are facing a difficult period when there is going to be great pressure on the government to protect home industries due to competition from

Customs Act
other countries-competition which will come from Japan and from West Germany, where they have longer working hours-if we did start a form of protection it could result in the same thing happening that happened in the thirties, when ultimately every country suffered because each country tried to protect its own industries.
Facing as we do a situation like that, the people of Canada felt that it would be very wise to keep in office a government that really believed in increasing trade and doing away with barriers to trade. On this question it has been suggested that the Liberal party has not worked in favour of lowering tariff barriers. I wish to give a few figures because I know the attempt is made from time to time to give the impression that the Liberal party has not lived up to its policy of lowering tariff barriers and barriers to trade since it came into office in 1935.

Mr. Speaker, when we
adjourned for the dinner recess I was about to indicate to the house, in partial answer to the question of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), where these figures came from so he could see that they were as close an indication of the situation as one could get without going into a tremendous amount of detail. Those figures I gave with regard to the trade of Canada, the relative rate of duty on all imports and also on dutiable imports is taken from volume I of Trade of Canada for the year ended December 31, 1952. It is a publication of the bureau of statistics.
The actual percentages I gave take the amount of customs duty paid on imports as indicating the fraction of the value of the imports, and indicate that that is the percentage of the duty paid. In other words it is a weighted figure. For example, the figure I gave with regard to 1935, namely that the average rate of duty on all imports was 15-3 per cent, indicated that the customs duty paid was 15-3 per cent of the value of the imports of that year. The average rate of duty on dutiable imports was 27 [DOT] 4 per cent, which indicated that the rate of duty paid was 27 [DOT] 4 per cent of the value of the goods imported. That went down, as I have already pointed out, to 9-8 per cent, being the average rate of duty charged on all imports in 1952, and 18-2 per cent, being the average amount charged on dutiable imports in that year. As I pointed out, that indicated that there had been a reduction, since the Liberals came into office, of about 33 J per cent, whether you take it on the basis of all imports or on the basis of dutiable imports.
The only thing I wish to say in conclusion is that if the government feel they must proceed with this bill. I urge them to consider putting it into effect for one year only. I suggest they do that for three or four reasons. One of them is this. I greatly doubt whether a law like this should be made a permanent law of our country. We might be prepared to pass it when we knew exactly the attitude of the government of the day toward interfering with trade, and the attitude of the minister in charge of its administration. However, if we pass it as a permanent law 83276-541
Customs Act
we may find a government in office which would have at their disposal a law with which they could cripple trade in a most devastating way. I therefore suggest that this house do no more than pass a law like this to have effect during a period of one year at a time, if it must be passed.
There is another reason why I make this suggestion. This is more or less a new departure. In effect it is authorizing the minister to impose a tax that he decides is proper under the authority of the law. It is going to be an extremely difficult tax to impose. I suggest that parliament should keep a tax like this under close control and have it in such a position that what has been done under this law should be reviewed as a matter of course if it is decided to keep it in force for another year. In other words the actual operations under a statute like this should be subject to review by parliament every year, just in the same way as we review the effect of other taxes when we consider the financial situation in the budget debate and on the various budget resolutions.
Then I also suggest this procedure for another reason. I do not suggest it would be so necessary with a minister of the experience of our present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) with his known ability to resist pressure, but I do suggest that it would be most helpful to a new minister who did not have his experience. The idea that would be impressed upon people who might be bringing great pressure to bear on the department and on the minister to take drastic action at times under this section was that anything done would have to be reviewed by parliament. It might assist the minister in resisting pressure to take too drastic action at any time if the people asking for it realized that, when the act came up for renewal, they might not get it renewed at all.
Therefore when we are passing a law like this I think it should be effective only for one year to begin with. We certainly should not decide on it as part of our permanent law until we are absolutely sure that it is possible to administer it, that it is not going to do more harm than good, and that it is capable of enforcement without interfering too much with the trade of the country.
I therefore urge that the minister give consideration to this act having effect for only one year from the date of enactment. If it turns out that it is useful and helpful, there will be no difficulty in getting it renewed; but certainly it will mean that this new departure will not have been written irretrievably into the law of the land. Surely the onus should be on those who want this change to be made. They should be willing

Customs Act
to have it tried for one year, and the onus should be on them to come back and ask for its renewal rather than on those who doubt the wisdom of its having to come and try to get it repealed. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when the time comes to put this bill through committee, it be restricted in its operation to one year.

I was touched this afternoon when, after referring to the danger of trade being strangled, he said that of course it never could be strangled in the good days of this government; but then after dinner apparently caution was stronger again, because I note that he now wishes it to be limited to one year and that he speaks of the possibility of it crippling trade in a devastating way.
There may be more truth in that statement than perhaps immediately meets the eye, because it may be that this clause could so upset, delay and slow up everything that it might cripple trade in a way which perhaps even the minister does not intend. However, that is something we can consider later.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Rosthern on doing his best to meet the various difficulties with which he is confronted and which he finds in his own makeup. It reminded me a little bit of the story of the chameleon who was put on a tartan; the poor little fellow burst.
This question of dumping is undoubtedly a matter of the very first importance, and it has been a matter of importance for a long time, although that fact does not seem to have been as clear to the government as it should have been. Churchill, we are told, was in the habit of sending around memoranda endorsed "Action this day". The minister could not do that, and I do not know what stamp the minister uses, but so far as this matter is concerned what we find is that it has not been a case of "action this day" but "action in 21 months." Let us be quite
[Mr. Tucker.)
clear what it is with which we are dealing. We are dealing not with tariffs but with dumping. We are dealing with a situation which arises almost wholly by reason of business action in the United States, and this has nothing to do with our relations with Great Britain at the present time.
In the New English dictionary we find this definition of dumping:
Dump. To import, or throw on the market, in large quantities and at low prices; specifically to offer for sale (surplus goods), especially abroad, at less than the ordinary trade prices.
It is rather interesting to note that the first quoted use of the word is to be found in the Congressional Record of 1884. In other words it was an American invention, and it is the present American use of the invention in which we are interested tonight.
Why has it come up after all these months of silence? I think the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) probably indicated one very good reason, namely that the shoe is beginning to pinch very near home.

I think, for example, that the speeches made not only this side but on the other side of the house within the last couple of weeks have also had their influence. There is no doubt about that. I am sure the minister and I need not have any falling out about that.
I would also think that the barrage to which the government has been subjected and which culminated to some extent in the recent visit by the textile union workers of America, who were received by the minister and some of his colleagues some two or three weeks ago-I am sure that had something to do with it also. Why would it not?
I should like to refer to the Globe and Mail of November 18, 1953, page 9, where there is a report of the meeting of the union with certain members of the cabinet. The head of the deputation, Mr. Daoust, accused the government of being evasive and of having failed to call a conference of government, management and labour representatives as the union had requested two years ago. That is 24 months ago and I said 21. I was conservative.

The ministers who assisted the Minister of National Revenue were not able to help him as much, I am sure, as they would have liked to. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was there and he was in one of his plain-spoken moods. He said in a very outright fashion:
I don't know how peacetime demand can be expected to take up the productive capacity needed in war.
That was a statement of fact, I should think, but I am sure it did not help the Minister of National Revenue very much at that moment. At page 337 of Hansard for March 11, 1952, the hon. member for Broadview said:
As there are a number of textile mills in my riding, I should like to add my voice in asking the government to take steps to alleviate what amounts to a real depression in the textile industry. The main cause of this depression is legalized dumping of American textiles. I shall explain what I mean. Mills in the United States supply a market fifteen to twenty times the size of the Canadian market. They make very large runs in order to take full advantage of mass production methods. As they cannot forecast exactly the yardage of a particular pattern or material that will sell, they make sure to over-run, rather than incur the high cost of setting up their machines a second time. The yardage in excess of what the United States market can absorb, at regular prices, must be disposed of. If it is sold at bargain prices on the United States market, it will slow down the absorption of new lines. It is therefore desirable to dispose of this excess yardage in outside markets; the closest of these being Canada.
In order to get around our anti-dumping laws, the United States mills make one small sale at a price far below the price at which the goods are regularly sold on the United States market. The goods are then disposed of in the Canadian market, at an artificially low price, which is usually well below the cost of production of the Canadian mills. The over-runs, which may be small in terms of the United States market, usually represent a large percentage of the Canadian market. It is this flooding of the Canadian market with dumped United States textiles that has caused Canadian textile workers to be laid off in very large numbers.
Bear in mind that this was March 11, 1952.
These unemployed textile workers cannot be re-employed until the mills which formerly employed them are once again able to compete on fair and even terms with the United States mills. That time will not come until the government makes sure that the prices of the United States textiles entering Canada are the regular prices at which the goods were sold on the United States market, and not a fire-sale price, offered to clear out over-runs.
That was the statement made by the hon. member for Broadview. It seems very clear to me, and I think everyone will recognize that it was true. Then the next day we had a series of statements from the minister, and I find them very difficult to reconcile. The only way I can reconcile them is to suggest that on that particular day the minister was suffering from a split personality. I never could understand what that is, but at any rate I suggest that might explain what I am now going to read. Mr. Speaker, my sole purpose in taking part in this debate at this time is to attempt to clear up.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two comments on this bill. In the first place, I think it is born of panic to cover a panicky condition in a trade that could itself have remedied the situation that has reached a climax. I speak now on behalf of another group of industrialists or producers who have done their best for many years to eliminate the conditions which apparently have caught up to the textile industry.
I refer to the fruit and vegetable growers of British Columbia. They have organized

themselves to produce at the lowest price, to supply the market at the lowest price and at the same time stay in business. Year after year they have come to Ottawa seeking some protection against dumping, some assistance against unfair competition, and every year they have been told the same thing, that there is little or nothing that can be done.
I am referring to the unfair competition of peaches, apricots, prunes, berries and all those things which are brought into this country at prices away below the cost of production. This year shiploads of processed cherries were brought in from Italy to compete with our own British Columbia cherries. We have asked for protection but have got nowhere.
I ask the minister to consider putting in this bill a clause which would protect fruits, vegetables and canned goods. I mention canned goods because the situation there is even worse than in the case of soft fruits and vegetables. We meet competition in canned goods from South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and other countries under conditions which to my mind are nothing less than dumping. The situation is getting gradually worse.
Last year in British Columbia we consumed approximately $5 million worth of soft fruits and vegetables, and I was startled to learn that over $3 million of that total was imported from the United States. The earlier marketing of their products enables them to ship fruits and vegetables to our markets, and we feel that some protection should be given. Time and time again we have asked the department to invoke the dumping laws, but the answer has been that they have not sufficient staff to check on prices in the United States. I know they have not sufficient staff to send a man to every packing house in California, Texas and Arizona to find out what is the actual cost of production. The customs officials at the borders are helpless. They have no idea what it costs to produce a ton of tomatoes or a ton of prunes. Therefore by default and through lack of knowledge these things are being dumped in our country.
I suggest to the minister that he consider right now adding a provision to the bill to prevent the dumping by other countries of canned goods, fruits and vegetables. If the minister will assure me that the bill will cover canned goods, fruits and vegetables I will be satisfied. But I will not be satisfied if they are not covered.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house were pleased last Monday when the
Customs Act
minister indicated that the government intended to take some action to try to stop the legalized dumping of American textiles in this country, which has been going on since 1948.
As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) said earlier, this matter was explained quite clearly to the minister nearly two years ago. At that time the minister said most emphatically that no dumping was going on, and he refused to have the matter investigated. But during the last two years this dumping of American textiles has gone along merrily, with the American exporters and importers using Canada as a happy dumping ground, and laughing up their sleeves at us and particularly at the Canadian government.
As I say, during the past two years the government have done nothing but persist in sitting on their Liberal posteriors. We now see them beginning to shake themselves into some action because of pressure brought to bear on two members of the government by employees in textile plants in their particular constituencies.
The trouble all started in 1948 when this government switched from the definition of fair market value which had prevailed up to that time, to a new definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Prior to 1948 the definition of fair market value, which appeared in section 36 of the old Customs Act, was as follows:
In no case shall fair market value for import purposes be less than the actual cost of production of similar goods at the date of shipment to Canada, plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit.
That definition of fair market value is the only possible workable definition for import purposes. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, and that definition made it impossible for dumping to take place in Canada up to that time.
Then in 1948, in order to comply with the GATT agreements-agreements which the United States exporters incidentally have not observed, either in spirit or in detail-we changed our definition of fair market value to something which bore no resemblance to

Customs Act
lair market value. And then, of all things, we allowed this definition to be formulated for us by the Department of Justice. A statement outlining this definition was made by the minister on March 12, 1952, as reported on page 359 of Hansard, as follows:
-a "fair market value" may bear no necessary relationship to production cost.
Anyone who has ever engaged in business, whether it be buying, selling, manufacturing or any other kind of effort, knows there is only one workable definition of market value, that is manufacturing cost, plus selling cost, plus administrative cost, plus a reasonable profit. No manufacturer or seller of goods has operated on any other basis than what he considered to be a reasonable profit. To accept the definition of the Department of Justice, that fair market value bore no relationship to manufacturing cost, was to me an utterly foolish and impractical thing. It has resulted in a very large volume of fire sale goods from the United States being dumped in this country during the past five years.
That definition has allowed the Americans to dispose of two types of distress merchandise: first of all, as the member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) described earlier, the kind which is the result of an over-run, as it was described to the minister some two years ago. United States mills deliberately over-run under industrial mass production methods, because they cannot bear the cost of a second set-up to make good the commitment to those they have contracted to supply.
In order that these excess goods do not clog the intake of new lines for the next selling season, they have to be disposed of in some market outside the country of origin, and the nearest, handiest dumping ground is Canada. Of course the United States mills have been aided by our government, which has simply allowed them to bring in goods on an invoice made out for one small sale at a fire sale price. What was taken as a fair market value had no relationship to the cost of production, and the goods arrived in Canada and competed with goods produced by our Canadian mills and by our Canadian workmen.
The other kind of distress merchandise has resulted from deliberate over-runs due to the fact that large mills relied for their efficiency on continuity of production, running twelve months of the year. If ten months' production would satisfy the total intake which the United States market could absorb, these mills were willing to keep on producing for the other two months at or below the cost of production, rather than see the efficiency of their machines and factories impaired.

I have talked about this matter, Mr. Speaker, to a number of United States businessmen, and asked them about the dumping operations. They freely admit this dumping. They laugh about it. They say, "We produce the goods and your government makes it easy for us to send the goods into Canada. There is nothing illegal about it. They have made it legal." It was from them that I acquired the term "legalized dumping", because that is exactly what they call it; and they laugh uproariously and say, "Of course, it is dumping. Your government invites us to do it, and we are protecting our American workmen. We do not care very much whether your Canadian workmen have jobs or not."
I do not like, and no member of my party, and I am sure no member of this house likes, to see any workman out of a job, but if it is necessary to have workmen out of jobs I would rather see them in Chicago, Atlanta or Milwaukee than in Montreal, Galt or Toronto. I say Canada first. The Americans say America first, and for the past five years we have let them get away with it, and our workers have suffered as a consequence.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
As regards the government's proposed legislation, it is now their intention to stop the dumping of United States textiles and other goods in this country by a formula whereby they are going to set a fair market value on the weighted average of sales in the United States market over the past six months.
That sounds like a very good solution when you hear it first. There is something very nice and workable about the phrase "a weighted average". But, Mr. Speaker, from a practical point of view, it is absolutely and completely unworkable. To start with, there are several classes of customers to whom producers in the United States sell. There are manufacturers who have to sell to other manufacturers. There are retailers, and there are jobbers. These classifications are further broken down into large accounts, medium accounts and small accounts. They all have different prices at which they buy from the original manufacturer.
Then there are further quantity discounts, and there are year-end rebates which a customer receives at the end of the year when he shows that he has bought a certain quantity of goods. When you add to these variations the many sizes, styles and patterns which can be brought into the picture, I think it is obvious that if you take all the various

types of sales that can be made, and the various qualities, sizes and so on, it is going to be a tremendous job in any one line to try to work out a weighted average over a six months period.
I think it would take several months to work out any weighted price, and an importer must know what the laid-down cost is immediately these goods land in Canada, for he buys these goods for immediate sale, especially in the case of style goods. If he waits until these investigations have been made, the selling season will be over and the goods will be of no use to him whatsoever.
If this kind of regulation is put into effect, it is going to make it impossible for an importer to import any goods unless they are simply staple products, in which case it doesn't matter how long they are held before sale. These types of goods are few in number.
I would urge the minister and his department to give this matter further study. I commend him for at long last having decided to take steps to curtail this dumping. It is a step in the right direction. My only quarrel with him is that I believe he is adopting the wrong method. I think it is a method that is unworkable, though, I am sure, well-meaning. It will cause great harm and delay, and block a large proportion of imports into this country.
That is not the purpose of this kind of legislation. Its sole purpose is to stop dumping. Legislation, to do that, must contain a workable definition of fair market value, which is the cost of production, plus selling costs, and administration costs, and plus a reasonable profit. If that definition of fair market value is returned to, then dumping can be effectively stopped, and it will not affect the other imports which we want to bring into this country at fair prices. I am sure that is the desire of all members in this house.
I know the members of my party are interested in defending the workers of this country against the breaches of the spirit of GATT which are being perpetrated at the present time by United States exporters. For that reason we are in favour of legislation to stop this dumping. I would again urge the minister to have another look at the method by which he proposes to do this, and before legislation is actually put into operation I hope he will give serious consideration to the points I have mentioned tonight.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this measure is put to the house there are a couple of questions to which I think we must address ourselves. I think we must consider, first, whether a case has been made
Customs Act
out for the legislation which is now before us and, second, whether it will have the effect which the government or the minister in charge believes it will have.
First of all I think it should be made clear that this measure means protection. Some of the speakers have gone to great pains to try to show that this is not a change in our tariff structure. Strictly speaking and perhaps technically speaking they may be right, but the practical effect of a measure such as this means higher customs duties. I do not believe that statement can be denied. We can put the situation into plain ordinary figures that are easy to read. For example, if we are now importing goods to the value of one dollar on which the customs duty is at the rate of 25 per cent, the government will have a rate of 25 cents on the dollar. But if the interpretation under this legislation is that that particular article should be valued at $2, that procedure automatically brings the customs duty to 50 cents instead of 25 cents. Therefore the practical effect of this legislation is exactly the same as an increase in tariff rates.
It was refreshing last night to hear the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who made no bones about where he stands and of course, if he spoke for his party, just where his party stands. He was for protection and, as far as I could interpret his speech, the more the better. At least he spoke in plain ordinary language that anyone could understand. But as the debate has gone along there has been a tendency to try to prove that this is not a change in our tariff structure. It does increase customs duties and to that extent it does restrict trade. But the question we must decide, it seems to me, is whether such a change is justified at this time. I have not heard the minister or anyone else on the government side or on any side of the house up to this point place the case for this change, in figures, before the house.
We are told that this matter has been brought to a head-and undoubtedly that is true-by the present conditions in the textile industry. Yet neither the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) nor anyone else I have heard so far has placed before the house figures which would prove that the textile industry is in such a position today that it requires this legislation. I realize that they made representations; but that was not the first time industries have made representations. The latest figures I can see, so far as investigations are concerned, are the reports handed down by the committee on prices which sat for I believe

Customs Act
two years and reported in 1948-I was a member of it for a period of time-and also the royal commission on prices which continued the work of that committee and reported, I believe, in 1949. According to those reports it would appear to me that the textile industry-if that industry is to be used as the excuse, as the foot in the door for a protectionist policy-has not exactly gone through the hardest times in the last few years.
I shall quote briefly from some of the reports. There is a great deal more available to anyone who is interested. For example, at page 3949 of the report it is pointed out that Courtaulds (Canada) Limited jumped their profits from $489,000 in 1946 to $1,434,000 in 1947. This went on year by year until 1950 or 1951. Further down on the page we find that Canadian Celanese Limited in 1946 made a net profit of $1,959,000 and by 1947 had jumped that profit to $3,025,000. When one of the representatives of the company was a witness before the committee and was questioned as to the possibility of reducing prices to the consumer owing to the very substantial margin of profit they were making at that time, he said they were not willing even to consider doing it. I quote now from page 3949 of the committee's report:
Mr. Palmer, of Canadian Celanese Limited, admitted that for the months of January, February, and March, 1948, the profits of that company were substantially higher than for the same period in 1947. In spite of that, the witness said that company increased its prices on April 1, 1948.
After admitting that their prices were much higher for the first three months of 1948 as compared with the previous, year, on April 1 of that year they did not reduce their prices but rather increased them. The report continues:
Asked whether in view of the very high profit of the company it would not be possible to reduce its prices Mr. Palmer definitely stated that there will be no reduction.
That was the attitude taken by those companies at that time when they were being investigated. They took the attitude that controls had been lifted, that this was a free-enterprise economy and that, to put it in different words, it was no one's business what kind of profits they made or what prices they charged. That is all very fine if they want to follow through with that sort of free-enterprise philosophy. But the moment they find that they have priced themselves out of the market, the moment they find that they have raised their prices to such a point that the volume of sales has fallen off and
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
that as a result their production is becoming curtailed, what do they do? They rush to the government and ask for a measure of protection. That procedure is hardly following through on their free-enterprise philosophy.
Referring now to the report of the commission which carried on the work of the committee substantially from the point where it was left off by the committee, we find the return on the capital of a group of these textile companies, as reported at page 255 of the report which I believe was made in 1949. We find that the 1942-45 average return on capital was 10 per cent, but that in 1946 it was jumped to 12-8 per cent, and that in 1947 that was again jumped to 22-3 per cent, or in other words it was more than twice as much as the average in the period 1942-45. Yet no move whatever was made to reduce prices.
May I just incidentally mention that after listening to all these statements made today about this dumping-one of the hon. members, coining a phrase, called it the happy dumping ground for the American companies -I am at a loss to know just where these goods are that have been dumped in Canada. I am sure there are many housewives who, now that they are doing their Christmas shopping, would be happy to find out where all those dumped cheap goods are, or where all those textiles are that are being sold in Canada at sacrifice prices. When we go out to buy a shirt, a pair of pajamas or a pair of socks, we find that the price is higher than it was before.
Where are all these things disappearing that are being dumped in Canada? Are we going to accept the government's word that there is a case for this amendment? I am not saying there is not, but I say no one has made out that case or has proven in this house that the textile industry is suffering owing to what is termed "dumping". They may be suffering as to volume of sales because of their own greedy policy of raising prices at a time when they were making enormous profits. By doing that they priced themselves out of the market, and are today reaping the benefit of their own policy.
Going further into this report of the royal commission, at page 256 we find this statement:
It seems evident that some of the work clothing manufacturers have received very high profits in 1947 and that part of the increased profits during 1947 might well have been passed along to the consumer.
But they were not passed on to the consumer. At page 261 of the same report they

refer to women's clothing and we find the following with respect to the return on shareholders' equity:
In the women's clothing, this return ranges from 9-9 per cent to 23-1 per cent, while in the children's clothing group, it goes from 13-0 per cent to 72-9 per cent.
These are not my words based on street corner gossip. These are words in the report of a royal commission set up by the government to investigate prices, and among the things they investigated were the prices charged and the profits made by the textile industry. So the house will not think I am picking on any particular companies, may I say that at page 262 of the report we find a group index which shows the position of these companies in various years. Taking 1945 as 100, we find that by 1946 their profits were 109-1, by 1947 187-5, and by April, 1948, when the report ends, 190-9.
All of this to me at least indicates that they were hardly in the position where they did not know where the next meal was coming from. Either a case can be made for this industry or it cannot. I for one wish to be openminded about the matter. I should like to hear someone make a case for the industry. We have heard a lot about dumping and various other things in this debate, but as far as I am concerned no one has made a case so far for the textile industry.
There is only one more thing I wish to say. In my opinion if any industry comes to the government asking for a measure of protection, which after all means taking money out of the consumer's pocket because it denies the consumer the lower price which he might otherwise get, it should be in a position to prove its case. In the second place, the government should protect the interests of the consumer and be prepared to exercise some control over the prices to be charged. It appears to me that we are in danger of having open-end arrangements where industries can benefit from protection and yet be uncontrolled and unrestricted as to the extent to which they can exploit the public. Apparently the textile industry is being used as a test case, and so far the government has not made a case for such protection for the industry.
So far as we are concerned, we are primarily interested in seeing that any benefits that may flow from such protection of the industry are passed on to the employees. There again we have no assurance from the government up to now that the employees in these industries are going to receive benefits commensurate with the benefits to the
Customs Act
companies themselves. We would like to be assured on these matters before this measure is put to a vote.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that I have the opportunity of following the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), because before I have finished my remarks I hope to be able to analyse and explain to the house and to the people of the Dominion of Canada why I and others from my riding have worked so hard to have this type of legislation put on the statute books.
Inasmuch as the hon. member for Dauphin is a member of the C.C.F. party, he amazes me tremendously. There has been no effort on the part of the government to enact any legislation whatever to give relief to the textile industry until it became a case of employment for labour. Every year during the past four years I have been in the house I have said at some time that the most important job of any government is to supply an opportunity for the people of the country to find jobs. If we have full employment we have good times, and when the hon. member for Dauphin suggests that we are introducing this legislation in order to give the textile manufacturers a chance to make more money I say that he is not familiar with the conditions at all. This legislation is being put in force in order to give the labourers of this country an opportunity to earn a living, and that is always the policy of the Liberal party.
I was also very pleased that the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) spoke. I like him to say that we are doing the right thing in the wrong way. His party has accused us of doing the right thing in the wrong way in the case of every piece of legislation we have put through in the past four years. I think the best instance of that which I can give is the Emergency Powers Act which was passed in the session of 1951. That was necessary. It had to be done. We had to do something about it.
