There is one thing with which I do not agree. This legislation is certainly not going to be a cure-all. It will provide a small benefit for the textile workers and also the storekeepers and the people who handle textile goods in the Dominion of Canada.
Following the plan of the hon. member for Dauphin, I should like to analyse the situation and explain why I have worked so hard to see that this legislation was brought in. One of the dress manufacturers in my town came to me a couple of years ago and suggested that with the Canadian dollar coming back to normal their business was being hurt, and we should do something about it. I said I sympathized with him, but I asked him whether he did not think it was time that the people in this country who buy goods got some of the advantages of our dollar coming back to par. Because they have got this benefit, I think it is opportune that I should suggest that the government deserves a little of the credit for bringing our dollar back to par.
I listened to this man very attentively, and I said, "If you can make out a case that I believe is logical and fair I will be only too glad to take you down to the Minister of National Revenue and to our good' friend, his assistant from Kitchener, and I am certain we will have a good hearing". We did not go, but last spring he came down to see me. He said, "Look, Henry, if you do not do something about this all our small shopkeepers right across the country are going to be hurt, and it is time you did something about it". I said, "Tell me the story, and if you have a story that we can take to the minister and the department, I am sure the minister will listen".
This was his story. A dress goods manufacturer in the United States manufactures several lines of dresses. Some of them sell and some of them do not. The ones that do not sell will be out of style next year, and so will be absolutely valueless. This manufacturer invites in the big buyers. There are only certain storekeepers in this country who can afford to have buyers in the United States, stores like Eaton's, Simpson's and

Hudson's Bay. Those concerns can afford to have buyers in this country, in the United States and even in England. Practically any steamship crossing the ocean will have a berth on it for buyers from Eaton's and Simpson's. These buyers are in a position to buy those articles that will go out of style. These styles do not catch the fancy of the ladies in the United States, so these buyers pick them up and you will see them listed in the seasonal catalogues and the daily papers published by these stores.
Those articles are brought into this country because they are not saleable in the United States. They could not be sold at the price over there, so the articles are brought into this country. They are sold by the manufacturer in the United States because he knows that if he does not get $1 instead of $10 at that time, he will not get a cent in two or three months' time. In the United States the season opens in March, and in Canada it opens in April. There is a month in which the manufacturer can try out the styles and see which ones are going to sell. Our market has been flooded with this inferior type of goods.
What has this done to the storekeepers who have no buyers in the United States, who are not able to go across and buy these grab-bag articles which can be put on sale to attract the public? They are in competition with this type of thing. I was told that unless we did something about this all the little shops alcng the main street of Guelph would be closed up. I told this gentleman that if he was prepared to come down to Ottawa with that story I was quite convinced that something would be done. I wish to thank the minister for the thought and the time that he has put into this measure.
In case someone thinks I am saying this measure will bring prosperity to the textile workers, let me say that I do not think that is the case. The same conditions apply in the case of knitted goods, hats and all those industries making seasonal goods. They are all affected in the same way as the case I cited about the dresses.
Let me tell my good friends in the C.C.F. party that there has been too much animosity created between labour and the manufacturer in this country. I come from the north country and I know of the damage that has been done in that part of the country by the gold strike. I know about the damage to the mines, the miners and the places where they live. Anyone who creates bad feeling between labour and management is doing a great disservice to this country. The thing we have to remember is that this measure will be of some help. I wish it could be more.

The only way we can get back into the textile business is for everybody to co-operate. The manufacturers have to be efficient. They have to have the best machines to do the best job. Labour has to work hard because we are in competition with people all over the world who are willing to work hard, and who have to work hard to get their daily bread. We have a fight on our hands in this textile industry, and although this legislation will help some it is not going to be a cure-all. There is no substitute for hard work. We have to have hard work on the part of management and on the part of labour if we are going to have jobs which will enable us to have the things we have enjoyed in the past.
Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de
Grace): I think perhaps it is encouraging to many of us to see the government giving some help to the textile industry, even though the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) does it rather in the way of arriving on a white horse, with his shoulder to the wheel, his ear to the ground and his finger on the pulse of the national economy; and that is a little bit difficult to do. I think it is almost as difficult as what he is proposing in his amendment to the act.
Perhaps I would have a little more trust and confidence in the ease with which the minister would carry this out if I did not recall a remark he made last week. At that time the minister said it was practically impossible to give a definition of what shall constitute machinery and apparatus used in the production of goods. After all, if the government does not know what machinery and apparatus is, how on earth are they going to be in a position to deal with all the problems and difficulties so adequately outlined earlier tonight by the member for Broadview (Mr. Hees)?
There is one other thing I might add. Earlier tonight someone to my left asked whether or not a case could be made out for the textile industry. I think it would be difficult not to make out a case for the textile industry. I think it would be difficult not to make out a case for any industry which is based on three simple statistics. It is an industry which employs approximately 100,000 people, an industry which produces some 700 million yards of fabric in the course of a year, an industry which has spent some $420 million in the last seven years in modernizing plant and equipment. I think those three figures give some little indication of the importance of this industry. Any person who tries to strike the ground from underneath that industry, from underneath the group of men
Customs Act
who have built it up, the group of men who have used the profits from their business to make a contribution to the Canadian economy, is certainly doing a disservice to this country. Anyone who criticizes that industry and says it has no place in Canada, that no case can be made for it, is doing a disservice to our whole economy and to the system under which we operate.
I would just close by saying that even though the horse may be somewhat spavined, it is good to have some measure of protection for our textile industry in Canada, inadequate though it may be.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. With regard to this matter of potatoes, I have the following suggestion to make that I should like the minister to take note of. In the Ladner area we grow early potatoes. In June of this year we had occasion to import California potatoes into British Columbia. The freight rate from California to Vancouver is $1.31 a hundredweight. California potato growers told us they grew those potatoes at $2 a hundredweight. However, they were selling them on the market at $1.10 a sack, which raised the price in British Columbia to $2.41 a hundredweight. In order for our growers to compete with them they would of necessity have to sell their potatoes at $2.41. They did sell them for less just to get rid of them; otherwise they would have been left with a large surplus and would not know what to do with them.
During the same period, because the Manitoba market was firmer, they had occasion to send 23 carloads from British Columbia to Manitoba. California also sent some potatoes to Manitoba. It is an interesting fact that the freight rate from Vancouver to Manitoba is $1.64 a hundredweight; the freight rate from California to Manitoba is $1.65 a hundredweight. It can easily be seen that the Californians would have been well advised to send their potatoes to Manitoba and allow the British Columbia potato growers to keep their own market for themselves.
If this dumping act that is proposed for manufacturers were applied to the potato growers we would find that the British Columbia potato growers would be much happier men than they are today. I am hoping the minister will see fit to have this act applied to both fruits and vegetables, because this situation is true not only of potatoes in British Columbia but it is also true of fresh fruits such as apricots and peaches, and the soft fruits such as strawberries and raspberries as well as general market garden production.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Is there anything the minister wishes to say? Will he trace for us the history of dumping since it began? It would be desirable to know just the main features, particularly during the years just before 1948, as I understand there was a change. Will he give us an outline?

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I think I can give you a complete history of dumping. The first provision for the collection of special or dumping duty was inserted in the Customs Tariff, section 19, effective on the 8th day of June, 1904, going back 50 years.
Briefly, the minister of customs or any officer of customs authorized to collect customs duty, when satisfied that the export price of any imported dutiable article of a class or kind made or produced in Canada was less than the fair market value thereof as determined under the Customs Act, was to collect a special duty of customs equal to the difference between such fair market value and such selling price. The special duty was not to exceed one-half of the customs duty otherwise established except in the case of certain primary iron or steel products on which the special duty was not to exceed 15 per cent ad valorem.
It is specially noted that this special duty was collectable only on dutiable goods, the only exemption being certain wire rods, which were free of duty and on which the special duty was not to exceed 15 per cent ad valorem.
The governor in council was authorized to impose special duty on goods shipped on consignment if satisfied that the goods were so shipped to evade special duty.
The minister of customs was authorized to make regulations for enforcement of the provision and had authority to make regulations for the temporary exemption of any article or class of articles if not made in Canada in substantial quantities and offered for sale to all purchasers on equal terms, and to exempt from special duty articles on which the ordinary duty was equal to or greater than 50 per cent ad valorem, or where the difference between the fair market value and the selling price of the goods only amounted to a small percentage of the fair market value. Goods subject to excise duty in Canada were not subject to special duty.
In the tariff of 1907, introduced on the 30th November, 1906, section 6 provided for the collection of special or dumping duty in addition to the duties otherwise established, and provided that such special duty be levied, collected and paid although the goods were not otherwise dutiable. It was also provided that such special duty should not exceed 15 per cent ad valorem and should
Customs Act
not apply to goods on which the duties otherwise established were equal to 50 per cent ad valorem, goods subject to excise duty, sugar refined in the United Kingdom and certain binder twine. Those were the exceptions.
It was also provided that excise duties in the country of export were to be disregarded in estimating the market value for the purpose of such duty when the goods were entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff.
The minister of customs still had power to make regulations similar to the provisions in the previous act. Note that the exemption of goods carrying duties equal to 50 per cent ad valorem were removed from the powers of the minister and were made statutory. That was in 1907.
By regulation, an exemption allowance of 5 per cent was provided for iron and steel and 7J per cent for other goods. In addition, advances in market value between date of purchase and shipment were disregarded.
From 1914 to 1929 various changes were made in the application of exemption allowances, and in 1929 they were finally withdrawn.
In 1930 a further change was made defining fair market value and raising the maximum special duty from 15 per cent to 50 per cent. Freight allowances similarly allowed in the country of export were disregarded for special duty purposes and an exemption was made for goods of a class subject to duty under the Excise Act. In the case of importations from Australia, the maximum was fixed at 15 per cent ad valorem, under the Australian trade agreement. It was also provided that excise duties and excise taxes should be disregarded in estimating the market value for the purposes of special duties when the goods were entitled to entry under any tariff more favourable than the general tariff, and that customs duties of the United Kingdom were to be disregarded in estimating the fair market value of wines for special duty when entitled to entry under any tariff more favourable than the general tariff.
In this amendment, authority of the governor in council to impose a special duty if satisfied that such special duty was being evaded by shipping goods on consignment was vested in the minister, and also to collect special duty in cases where a person imported goods for further manufacture or assembly or for resale, and subsequently sold them at prices below the duty paid value, plus freight and other charges.

Customs Act
In 1933, the governor in council was authorized to fix the rate of exchange for depreciated currencies.
Effective May 2, 1936, section 6 was again amended to provide that articles could be exempted from special or dumping duty when it was established that, although of a class or kind made in Canada, they were not offered for sale through the ordinary agencies of wholesale or retail distribution or were not offered to all purchasers under like conditions having regard to the customs and usages of trade. That was in 1936. It was effective May 2, so it would be under a Liberal government. The governor in council was also authorized to determine the percentage of Canadian production necessary to classify goods as of a class or kind made in Canada, and this was fixed at 10 per cent.
In 1937 the governor in council was authorized to fix the rate of exchange for appreciated currencies and was also authorized to order that import, excise or other duties and taxes imposed in any country may be disregarded in estimating the market value for special duty purposes.
By order in council, 19th December, 1941, under authority of the War Measures Act the imposition of special or dumping duty was suspended for the time being, except in respect to fresh fruit and vegetables. This suspension expired with the expiry of the War Measures Act on April 1, 1947.
In 1948, effective 19th May, the then existing section 6 was repealed and re-enacted, as revised, to conform to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. The new enactment, still in effect, provides that the basis for dumping duty shall be the fair market value or the value for duty of the goods as determined under the Customs Act, and the amount of special duty shall be the difference between the value for duty and the selling price to the purchaser in Canada. The value for duty provisions of the Customs Act were also amended to conform to GATT. That is what obtains at the present time.
The mandatory imposition of special duty within the provisions of the section, or authorized regulations thereunder, is continued in respect to all imported goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, whether free or dutiable, and with the limitation of 50 per cent ad valorem. It will be noted that when you add the dumping duty it cannot go up more than 50 per cent.
The authority of the governor in council to fix a rate of exchange for appreciated or depreciated currencies and the liability to dumping duty was withdrawn. This was in line with the amendment of section 55 of the Customs Act which provided for currency

values as declared by the Bank of Canada; and in the absence of such declaration the values may be determined by the minister as effectively reflecting the value of currencies in commercial transactions.
The new section provides that duties and taxes imposed in any country of export shall be disregarded in estimating the value for special duty purposes. This superseded the prior statutory authority for disregarding excise duties or excise taxes in respect to goods entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff, intermediate tariff or any tariff more favourable than the general tariff, and also superseded the statutory authority for disregarding customs duties of the United Kingdom in respect to wines when entitled to entry under the intermediate tariff or any tariff more favourable than the general tariff, when bottled in bond in the United Kingdom and imported direct therefrom. Also superseded was the authority of the governor in council to order disregard of import, excise or other duties and taxes, in whole or in part, in respect to goods of any kind imported from any specified country.
The new section continued ministerial authority to impose dumping duty in respect to goods shipped on consignment to evade this additional duty, and subsequently sold in Canada at prices representing less than the value for duty plus all charges after shipment, including sales, distribution and advertising costs and the cost of processing, assembling or further manufacture in Canada.
The exemption from special duty of goods subject to excise duty in Canada, which has been in effect since the dumping duty section was first instituted in 1904, is continued.
The requirement that goods shall not be deemed to be of a class or kind produced in Canada unless made in substantial quantities, and the authority for the governor in council to declare the quantities to be considered as substantial, is continued. The order in council requiring 10 per cent of Canadian consumption is still in effect.
The new statute also continued authority for deeming goods as of a class or kind not produced in Canada and exempt from special duty, where similar goods of Canadian production are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of distribution or offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions having regard to the custom and usage of trade.
A new provision was introduced in 1948 exempting goods or classes of goods declared exempt by any order or regulation made by the governor in council. Under this authority, the following goods were temporarily declared exempt. It goes on and gives a list,

and amongst these are motor vehicles, except those adapted for passenger use with seating capacity for more than ten persons, effective May 19, 1948, and withdrawn May 31, 1951. Then there is linoleum, oilcloth, confectionery, sanitary earthenware, lawn mowers, white Portland cement, etc.
The regulations providing for the following exemptions have been continued: Bona fide samples, advances in the market value after purchase, cash discounts, freight allowances, deferred quantity allowances and job lots, seconds, etc.

not perhaps in full detail but in general, the amounts of anti-dumping duties that have been collected and chiefly from what countries? I just wish to have a general idea of what the history has been.

I cannot give you the figures for different countries, but for the past five years the dumping duties on importations into Canada have been, in round figures, in 1948, $1,343,000; in 1949,	$1,673,000; in 1950,
$1,735,000; in 1951, $1,547,000; and in 1952, $1,373,000.
I think the hon. member will see from these figures that very close scrutiny has been given to invoices as they came along, and if we believed that the values were abnormally below normal the dumping duty was applied. That has been applied not only to the United States but in some instances to Great Britain, Japan, Czechoslovakia and these other countries, so there is general application and the amount of duties collected in these years has run to $8 or $9 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: I think the years the minister has referred to were the years we had a seller's market. I am interested in the previous years when the amounts are very much larger. Did I understand the minister to say it was $8 or $9 million in some years?

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: I would like to go back to the years when we were suffering, and learn what the anti-dumping duties were then. There is no year in which the duties amounted to $9 million. The figures

I misunderstood the minister on that point. It was no doubt the total I heard. But I would like to have the figures going back for some time, and I would like to have an idea of whether this has always been largely a United States problem. Perhaps the minister could give us these figures on Monday.

speechtext: Of course, Mr. Chairman, dumping was not in operation before the years of the war and we cannot give figures for those years.

speechtext: I am afraid I have not made my question clear. I think there was a change made in the year 1948, and I would like the minister to tell us what circumstances caused that change.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
